Correlate calendar event title retrieval with Base64 decoding operations or suspicious URL construction activity.

suggestion.title: Developer Credential and Wallet File Enumeration
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware 'stole cryptocurrency wallets and developer credentials'. Detection should target suspicious file access on credential and wallet storage locations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for process access to ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, ~/.git, ~/.vscode/globalStorage, cryptocurrency wallet directories (e.g., .metamask, .ethereum), and browser credential stores initiated by VSCode extensions or their child processes. Alert on enumeration followed by archival or network exfiltration.

suggestion.title: Extension Malicious Activation on Package Update
suggestion.rationale: Article notes 'Glassworm operators planted dozens of dormant extensions on OpenVSX that would activate the malicious component after an update'. This persistence mechanism exploits the extension lifecycle.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor VSCode extension update processes for unusual child process spawning or capability execution post-update. Detect extensions marked as dormant or disabled that spawn executables or make network connections immediately following an update cycle. Track extension activation version mismatches.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Package Repository Injection Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly names a supply chain attack infrastructure takedown; the article likely describes malicious packages injected into developer repositories. No detection coverage was generated despite this being a primary attack surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unsigned or unexpectedly-signed binaries pulled from package managers (pip, npm, NuGet, Maven); alert on mismatched file hashes, unexpected version rollback, or rapid re-publication of known packages. Correlate with source IP geolocation anomalies relative to project maintainers.

suggestion.title: Malware-Signed Developer Tool Execution
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attacks typically compromise build tooling or IDE integrations. Pipeline should detect execution of developer tools signed by non-standard or newly-issued certificates post-compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for Visual Studio, npm, gcc, Maven, or .NET tools executed with recent or unusual code signatures; alert on tools loaded from temp directories, user profile roots, or non-standard package cache locations.

suggestion.title: Registry Autostart Persistence via Build Artifacts
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain malware typically plants persistence in developer workflows via autostart mechanisms. No persistence detection was offered despite the target being developers with elevated system privs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and HKLM equivalents modified during or after package installation; correlate with recent installer execution or build system triggers.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Child Process Launch from Package Manager or Build Tool
suggestion.rationale: GlassWorm malware would likely execute secondary payloads from npm, pip, or build runners. Pipeline should detect process spawning that violates known safe behavior of package managers.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline of legitimate child processes spawned by npm.exe, pip.exe, dotnet.exe, maven.exe; alert on cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wmic.exe, certutil.exe, or unknown executables spawned from those parents outside expected build contexts.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement from Developer Workstation to Internal Network
suggestion.rationale: Compromised developer machines are high-value targets for lateral movement into corporate networks. No detection was generated for post-compromise reconnaissance or lateral movement tactics.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on network enumeration tools (nmap, ipconfig /all, nltest, net view) or credential theft utilities (mimikatz, secretsdump) executed from developer toolchains or package manager parent processes.

suggestion.title: DLL Side-Loading via Benign Utility Download
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'archive includes the legitimate executable for the legitimate utility as well as a malicious DLL that is automatically loaded when launching the benign binary.' This is a primary compromise mechanism.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for legitimate utilities (CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, etc.) spawning from user-writable or temporary directories and loading DLLs not signed by expected publishers. Detect mismatched directory provenance (e.g., CrystalDiskInfo launched from AppData or Temp rather than Program Files).

suggestion.title: msiexec.exe Executing Remote Access Tool Installers
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'DLL uses msiexec.exe to install vcredist_x64.dll, which is a package installer for the ScreenConnect remote access tool.' Suspicious msiexec child processes installing remote access software.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on msiexec.exe spawning from unsigned or suspicious parent processes (DLLs, PowerShell), or invoking ScreenConnect, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, or similar remote access installers. Focus on msiexec with /quiet or /qn flags and non-standard source paths.

suggestion.title: Process Hollowing into Signed Microsoft .NET Binaries
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies: 'process hollowing into a legitimate .NET binary signed by Microsoft: InstallUtil.exe, RegAsm.exe, RegSvcs.exe, MSBuild.exe, AppLaunch.exe, AddInProcess.exe, aspnet_compiler.exe.' These binaries are abuse targets.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for these specific signed binaries spawning unexpected child processes (network activity, file access, GPU miners) or receiving process injection signals. Flag parent processes known for hollowing delivery (PowerShell, rundll32). Detect memory manipulation patterns targeting these executables.

suggestion.title: Microsoft Defender Exclusion Modification via PowerShell
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'malware...invokes PowerShell to add its path and process to the exclusion list in Microsoft Defender.' Direct defense bypass via exclusion list tampering.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on PowerShell (especially -NoP, -Hidden, -Enc variants) executing Add-MpPreference, Set-MpPreference, or registry modifications to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions. Flag any Defender exclusion changes from non-admin/non-system accounts.

suggestion.title: ScreenConnect Service Installation and Unexpected Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Article highlights: 'deploying the legitimate remote management ScreenConnect tool...persistent access on the machine' as key to the attack. ScreenConnect is installed post-compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect ScreenConnect installation via msiexec or unusual installation paths, particularly when spawned from non-interactive or malware-associated parent processes. Monitor for ScreenConnect service creation without user action, especially via remote script delivery or lateral movement.

suggestion.title: VM Detection and Analysis Tool Process Enumeration
suggestion.rationale: Article notes: 'malware checks the environment for virtual machines and a set of 40 process names corresponding to analysis tools. If any are identified, the malware terminates its execution.' Defensive sandbox/analysis evasion.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on processes enumerating 40+ analysis tools (Process.GetProcessesByName loops), querying WMI for VM indicators (Win32_ComputerSystemProduct, Hyper-V classes), or checking for debugging/reversing tools (x64dbg, IDA, WinDbg, Procmon, Wireshark). Flag rapid process enumeration bursts from unsigned binaries.

suggestion.title: Grandoreiro/BTMOB Malware Execution via PowerShell or CMD
suggestion.rationale: Article title indicates active Grandoreiro and BTMOB campaigns; these families are known for process-injection and script-based execution on Windows. No execution-phase detection rules generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for child processes spawned from explorer.exe, rundll32.exe, or cmd.exe with characteristics typical of banking-trojan loaders. Grandoreiro variants often use WMI or PowerShell for lateral movement. Flag anomalous script execution with system-binary obfuscation patterns.

suggestion.title: Credential Access via Clipboard/Keylogging Indicators
suggestion.rationale: Banking trojans like Grandoreiro explicitly target financial credentials; article discusses 'campaigns' implying credential harvesting. No credential-access phase coverage generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on processes with clipboard/input-capture API calls (kernel-mode hooking of GetClipboardData, SetClipboardData). Flag repeated failed login attempts (credential stuffing) immediately following malware execution artifacts. Monitor browser session hijacking via injected hooks.

suggestion.title: Command & Control (C2) Communication Patterns
suggestion.rationale: BTMOB is explicitly described as a RAT; Grandoreiro uses C2 for remote task execution. Pipeline generated no command-and-control detection use cases.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect outbound connections to non-standard ports (>10000) or encrypted tunnels from infected hosts. Identify DNS requests for newly registered or previously unused domains resolved post-infection. Flag repeated reconnection attempts to same C2 IP/hostname with jitter.

suggestion.title: Android Malware Installation and Persistence (BTMOB)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions Android targets for BTMOB RAT campaigns; no Android-specific persistence or execution rules generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for sideloaded APK installations outside Google Play, particularly those requesting SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, READ_CONTACTS, READ_SMS, or RECORD_AUDIO permissions. Flag app processes with background service persistence and network outbound activity post-installation.

suggestion.title: Registry Persistence Hooks (Grandoreiro Windows)
suggestion.rationale: Banking trojans maintain persistence via registry modifications and scheduled tasks; no persistence-phase detection for Windows implants generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on modifications to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon (Userinit, Shell, Notify) and HKLM registry paths associated with AppInit DLLs. Monitor scheduled task creation with random-name patterns or system-service impersonation.

suggestion.title: Process Injection and Memory-Resident Execution
suggestion.rationale: Both families use process hollowing and code injection to evade detection; no defense-evasion or memory-resident detection rules generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate suspicious parent-child process relationships (e.g., svchost.exe spawning unusual children). Flag LoadImage events for unsigned DLLs injected into system processes. Monitor for process memory writes via WriteProcessMemory API with elevated privilege context.

suggestion.title: Malware Downloaded via AI Chatbot Recommendation
suggestion.rationale: Article title: 'Hackers Abuse AI Chatbot Recommendations to Push Malicious Software Download Links.' Pipeline extracted zero use cases despite this being the core attack. Users following chatbot-suggested links to download malware is executable execution + social engineering.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for file downloads (especially .exe, .msi, .zip) occurring within minutes of user ChatGPT/Claude/other-AI-chatbot sessions and subsequently executed. Cross-correlate browser history or application logs showing chatbot access, then flag downloads to low-reputation or unknown domains. EDR execution logs confirm follow-on malware behavior.

suggestion.title: Anomalous AI Chatbot Recommendation Output Detection
suggestion.rationale: Attack requires 'hackers [to] abuse AI chatbot recommendations'—implies attacker-controlled prompts or model manipulation steering users to malicious links. No detection for corrupted/injected chatbot responses.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect outlier chatbot responses: recommendations for software with no training-data precedent, repeated identical links across unrelated conversations, or domains flagged as malware sources appearing in system prompts or suggestions. Baseline normal recommendation patterns and flag statistical deviations.

suggestion.title: Known Malware Domains in AI Chatbot Context
suggestion.rationale: Article describes malicious download links distributed via chatbots. Pipeline must detect when known malware distribution domains appear in AI chatbot outputs or are accessed immediately after chatbot sessions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Maintain threat-intel feed of malware distribution domains known to be promoted in chatbot contexts. Alert on DNS/network queries to these domains when preceded by chatbot access logs within same user session. Correlate with file downloads and execution telemetry.

suggestion.title: User Execution of Malware File Following AI Service Interaction
suggestion.rationale: Core attack path: user trusts chatbot recommendation, downloads file, executes it. No use case maps this kill-chain step despite it being the most critical detection opportunity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag process execution of recently-downloaded binaries (age < 5 min) with low file reputation, especially if the download source is a domain flagged in threat intel as malware-distribution or if domain was recommended in prior chatbot session. Include command-line analysis and parent-process verification.

suggestion.title: Malicious npm Package Installation with Suspicious Child Process
suggestion.rationale: Article states '22 versions of npm RAT'—no detection logic for package installation followed by unexpected process spawning or network callbacks from node runtime.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm install/npm ci operations followed immediately by child process creation (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, etc.) spawned from node.exe or npm.exe parent, especially paired with network connections to non-standard infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Node.js Remote Access Trojan Command-and-Control Callback
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies 'persistent backdoor'—implies C2 infrastructure and callback behavior. No detection for node processes establishing unexpected outbound connections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on node.js processes initiating connections to non-whitelisted destinations outside npm registry, GitHub, and known package mirrors; flag connections on high ports (8000+) or to newly-registered domains correlated with package installation timestamps.

suggestion.title: Wallet and Credential File Access from Node Modules Context
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'wallet theft' capability—no detection for node processes accessing .env files, cryptocurrency wallets (MetaMask, Exodus), browser credential stores, or SSH keys.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for file access from node.exe/npm.exe processes targeting %APPDATA%\Local\{MetaMask,Exodus,Brave}, user .env files, .ssh directory, .aws credentials, or browser LocalStorage/IndexedDB paths containing wallet seeds or API keys.

suggestion.title: Persistence Mechanism in npm package.json Post-Install Hooks
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies 'persistent backdoor'—no detection for npm lifecycle script abuse (postinstall, preinstall, prepare) embedding C2 or scheduled execution logic.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag execution of scripts within node_modules/.bin/ outside of npm install context; alert on package.json modifications adding obfuscated post-install scripts; detect scheduled tasks or Startup folder entries launching node.js with malicious package dependencies.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Attack—Lookalike or Hijacked npm Package Detection
suggestion.rationale: Title indicates '22 versions' suggesting rapid version churn or multiple variants of same payload. No detection for package metadata anomalies, suspicious dependencies, or typosquatting patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cross-reference installed packages against npm registry metadata to flag: (1) packages with >5 versions released in <30 days; (2) packages with novel post-install binaries not in prior versions; (3) dependency trees including newly-created upstream packages or packages from low-reputation registries.

suggestion.title: Data Exfiltration from Developer Machine Post-RAT Infection
suggestion.rationale: RAT campaign targeting developer machines via npm supply chain implies theft of source code, credentials, or intellectual property. No detection for beaconing or bulk data transfer.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for repeated DNS requests from developer workstations to suspicious domains; flag large data transfers (>100MB) from affected machines to external IPs, especially encrypted HTTPS traffic on non-standard ports occurring shortly after npm package installation.

suggestion.title: Unsigned Installer Execution with Mismatched Publisher Metadata
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Fake ChatGPT and Claude Installers'—attackers deliver via unsigned or fraudulently-signed executables impersonating legitimate brands. Pipeline missed the need to detect publisher name/certificate mismatches for installer executables.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on executables with filenames containing 'ChatGPT', 'Claude', 'OpenAI', or 'Anthropic' paired with unsigned/revoked code signatures or publisher metadata not matching known legitimate vendors. Trigger if executed from user-writable paths (Downloads, Temp, %AppData%). Track hash of installer against known malware repositories.

suggestion.title: DinDoor Malware Process and Service Installation Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article names 'DinDoor Backdoor' as the payload—pipeline extracted zero mention of this malware family. Detection rules must monitor for DinDoor-specific process names, service installations, registry persistence mechanisms, and file artifacts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for DinDoor-associated process names, command-line arguments, or image paths. Alert on suspicious Windows service installations (NewService events) or registry modifications to HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services or Run keys written immediately after installer execution. Cross-reference against public DinDoor YARA rules and hash IOCs.

suggestion.title: Browser-Initiated Installer Download from Suspicious or Spoofed Domains
suggestion.rationale: Fake installer attacks rely on social engineering to download binaries from attacker-controlled or compromised domains. Article implies 'hackers use [fake installers]'—pipeline should detect atypical download sources for installer-named files.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag download of files with names matching 'ChatGPT', 'Claude', or generic installer patterns (Setup*.exe, Install*.msi) from domains not matching known legitimate vendor CDNs or official websites. Correlate browser network events with file writes to user temp/download directories. Alert if domain uses dynamic DNS, newly registered, or lacks valid SSL issuer trust chain.

suggestion.title: DinDoor Command-and-Control Beaconing and Callback Traffic
suggestion.rationale: Backdoor requires persistent C2 communication. Article states 'Deploy DinDoor Backdoor'—pipeline should generate detection for C2 channels once malware is resident, but extracted no network or C2 IOCs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for outbound network connections from DinDoor process space to known or suspected C2 infrastructure. Alert on suspicious beacon patterns (regular intervals, unusual ports, uncommon protocols). Cross-reference source and destination against threat feeds and sinkhole data for DinDoor family. Track TLS certificate SNI mismatches and HTTP User-Agent anomalies.

suggestion.title: Installer-to-Payload Execution Chain: Archive Extraction and Child Process Spawning
suggestion.rationale: Multi-stage installer attacks typically decompress/extract embedded malware then execute it. Pipeline missed behavioral sequence detection for installer delivery chain (download → extract → execute with elevated context).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate: (1) unsigned installer execution in user writable path, (2) followed by temp file creation/extraction (7z, WinRAR, Windows built-in archive expansion), (3) followed by child process execution (especially services.exe, svchost.exe, or rundll32.exe spawning suspicious binaries). Alert if child process requests elevated privilege or system file write access shortly after parent installer runs.

suggestion.title: Grandoreiro Process Execution with Registry Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Article title identifies Grandoreiro as the attack vector but pipeline generated zero use cases. Banking trojans establish persistence through registry modifications and process execution; title alone establishes this attack step.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for suspicious process creation in system directories and registry modifications to Run/RunOnce keys, AppInit_DLLs, or WinLogon entries. Detect parent-child process relationships inconsistent with legitimate Windows behavior.

suggestion.title: Credential Access via Banking Application Injection
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly targets 'Portuguese Banks and Latin American Companies'—hallmark of credential-stealing malware. Pipeline failed to surface detections for API hooking, screen capture, or keystroke logging against banking applications.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect API hooking (SetWindowsHookEx), screen capture (BitBlt, GDI), or keylogging libraries injected into banking or browser processes. Monitor for LSASS credential access attempts or legitimate banking apps with unusual child processes.

suggestion.title: Command and Control Beaconing Patterns
suggestion.rationale: Grandoreiro requires C&C communication for command delivery and data exfiltration—core attack step implicit in the malware family name. Pipeline generated zero network-based detections despite this being standard banking trojan behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for periodic HTTP/HTTPS outbound connections from suspicious processes with suspicious user-agents or to newly registered domains. Detect DNS queries for infrastructure domains associated with known Grandoreiro campaigns or similar banking trojan families.

suggestion.title: Process Injection and Code Execution Evasion
suggestion.rationale: Banking trojans universally employ remote process injection (CreateRemoteThread, WriteProcessMemory) to hide in legitimate processes. This defense evasion technique is standard for Grandoreiro but pipeline surfaced no detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect remote process creation and memory writes from non-system binaries into system or banking processes. Monitor for disablement of Windows Defender, UAC bypass attempts, or API hooking to avoid detection.

suggestion.title: Screen Capture and Clipboard Data Exfiltration
suggestion.rationale: Banking trojans capture screens and clipboard data during user login sessions. Article context (targeting banks) establishes this collection phase; pipeline generated zero detections for data harvesting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect screen capture and clipboard access APIs (BitBlt, GetClipboardData) called by non-admin processes. Correlate suspicious API calls with outbound network connections or file writes to identify credential/session data harvesting.

suggestion.title: Malware Delivery and Execution via Email or Web
suggestion.rationale: No initial-access detection offered. Article targets Portuguese banks and Latin American companies—likely phishing or malvertising delivery. Pipeline should have suggested detections for malware distribution vectors.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for macro-enabled Office documents, suspicious attachments, or executables executed from browser temp directories. Detect Office application child processes spawning system binaries or LOLBins.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Package Installation from Unofficial Registry
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states 'Legitimate-Looking' package that is malicious—supply-chain compromise via package registry is the attack vector. Pipeline missed initial-access detection entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect npm/pip installations from non-standard registries, packages with typosquatting patterns (character substitution, hyphen confusion), or packages published minutes before install attempt. Correlate with lack of commit history or repo authenticity signals.

suggestion.title: Credential Harvesting from Environment Variables
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions 'Steals Your AI Tokens'—detection for unauthorized read of $OPENAI_API_KEY, $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, or similar environment variables from package install scripts is critical gap.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag package install scripts (package.json postinstall, setup.py, requirements.txt hooks) accessing environment or reading ~/.bash_profile, ~/.ssh, or credential stores. Baseline legitimate credential access and alert on anomalies.

suggestion.title: API Token Exfiltration to Unknown Destination
suggestion.rationale: Article describes token theft; pipeline missed detection of credential transmission. Title establishes data exfiltration as the impact phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTPS POST/GET requests containing OpenAI, Anthropic, or AWS API key patterns (base64-encoded, 'sk-' prefix, 'Bearer' tokens) sent to non-whitelisted domains. Correlate with recent package install + unexpected outbound connection.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized API Usage from Installation Context
suggestion.rationale: Once tokens are stolen, attacker uses them—detection of API calls originating from the compromised package process or scheduled tasks running under install context would catch exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for spike in API token usage from new/unknown IP addresses, geographies inconsistent with org footprint, or times outside business hours. Cross-reference token creation timestamp with install date.

suggestion.title: Package Install Script Runtime Anomalies
suggestion.rationale: Malicious postinstall hook execution is the execution phase—pipeline did not suggest detection for suspicious child processes spawned by npm/pip/setup.py.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when package install spawns unexpected children: curl/wget downloading scripts, base64 decoding, compression utilities, reverse shells, or process modification tools. Baseline per package; flag deviations.

suggestion.title: Persistence via Package Initialization Hooks
suggestion.rationale: For sustained token theft, malware likely persists via hooks in application startup or scheduled tasks—pipeline omitted persistence-phase detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for modifications to package.json scripts, cron jobs, systemd timers, or application initialization code that invoke the compromised package. Alert on persistent callback mechanisms established during install.

suggestion.title: npm Package Install with Suspicious Postinstall Script Activity
suggestion.rationale: Article describes malicious npm package — postinstall scripts are standard attack vector for npm packages to execute arbitrary code during installation without user awareness. No UC generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor node.js process spawning child processes or making network connections immediately after npm install command. Flag postinstall scripts invoking curl, wget, or PowerShell to exfiltrate data. Alert on npm_modules/.bin/* executing binaries with unusual parent process.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Access to Claude AI Config/Cache Directories
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'stole files from Claude AI user directory' — implies discovery and access to ~/.claude or similar application config paths containing sensitive data. Pipeline did not model collection phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on any process (especially node.js children) attempting file enumeration or stat() calls on ~/.claude*, ~/.config/claude*, or %APPDATA%\Claude* directories. Flag recursive directory traversal of home directory initiated from npm context.

suggestion.title: npm Child Process Exfiltration to GitHub or External Host
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions 'via GitHub' implying C2 or data exfil routing through GitHub (possibly gist, raw content, or API abuse). Kill-chain reconstruction completely omitted exfiltration phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor DNS requests and outbound connections from npm/node processes to github.com, api.github.com, gist.github.com or attacker-controlled C2 domains. Flag curl/wget invoked with GitHub URLs concatenated from exfiltrated data filenames or base64-encoded payloads.

suggestion.title: Anomalous npm Package Metadata or Dependency Injection
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline did not attempt to extract the actual malicious package name, version, or hash — should surface package.json modifications, typosquatting variants, or dependency confusion patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm registry queries and local package.json writes for newly-added dependencies with names similar to popular packages (e.g. 'claudeai' vs 'claude-ai'). Alert on package downloads from npm CDN with unusual file sizes or install-time modifications to node_modules.

suggestion.title: Process Privilege Context Mismatch: npm Module Accessing User Directories
suggestion.rationale: If npm package running as regular user or in build context suddenly accesses ~/.claude or other sensitive user config, indicates either privilege escalation or explicit collection. Pipeline did not map this privilege/scope violation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate npm process UID/GID with file access ACLs — alert if a build-context npm module (or node process with restricted token) successfully reads files from different user's home directory or system-protected paths. Flag use of sudo/RunAs within postinstall scripts.

suggestion.title: npm Package Masquerading as Legitimate Dependency
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain attacks rely on naming deception (typosquatting, namespace confusion). Article title alone suggests package was malicious but nameSquatting detection is absent from pipeline output.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Compare package names in package-lock.json against known legitimate packages; flag visually-similar names or packages from new/unvetted publishers. Monitor npm audit/security alerts for flagged packages and correlate with DevOps/CI infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Preinstalled App Interfering With Third-Party App Traffic
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Preinstalled App Found Hijacking Amazon App to Inject Affiliate Codes' — pipeline failed to generate detection for one app intercepting/modifying another app's network traffic or parameters.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect system/vendor-signed apps spawning child processes or establishing hooks that intercept outbound traffic from known commerce apps (Amazon, eBay, etc.). Monitor for process injection, library loading, or API hooking from privileged system apps into user-installed applications.

suggestion.title: OEM Supply Chain Compromise - Malicious Preinstall
suggestion.rationale: Article core claim: 'Motorola Phones Preinstalled App' — supply-chain compromise at manufacturing/OS build level. Pipeline did not surface T1195 or T1195.001.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify unexpected system partition or /system/app installed applications on OEM devices absent from baseline manifests. Correlate app signatures and behavioral patterns (network outbound, inter-process communication, privilege requests) against known legitimate OEM vendors.

suggestion.title: Transaction Hijacking - Affiliate Code Injection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states injection of 'Affiliate Codes' into Amazon transactions. No detection for modification of payment/commerce parameters, merchant URLs, or referral tags.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP requests from commerce apps for anomalous URL parameters: unexpected 'tag', 'ref', 'affiliate', or 'partner' parameters; unexpected domain redirects; or modification of legitimate merchant URLs to include attacker-controlled identifiers.

suggestion.title: Vendor-Signed App Exceeding Declared Capabilities
suggestion.rationale: Preinstalled apps possess elevated privilege and can perform cross-app manipulation not disclosed in manifest. Article implies capability abuse to intercept another app's traffic.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag system apps accessing APIs, manipulating file descriptors, or performing operations that exceed their declared manifest permissions, particularly network interception, app inspection, or IPC capabilities.

suggestion.title: Beaconing from Bundled Apps to Affiliate/Ad Networks
suggestion.rationale: Malicious preinstalled app likely establishes C2 or monetization backend connections. Article does not detail infrastructure but baseline should capture unexpected outbound from system apps.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline legitimate OEM apps' network egress. Alert on persistent or periodic connections from system/preinstalled apps to domains associated with affiliate networks, ad exchanges, or monetization platforms not matching regional context or user profile.

suggestion.title: Chatbot Recommendations to Suspicious/Malicious Domains
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'AI Chatbot Recommendations Redirect Users to Cryptojacking Malware Sites' — chatbot output anomalies and redirection to known-malicious infrastructure are the core attack vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor chatbot API responses and rendered recommendations for URLs matching known cryptojacking malware domains, C2 infrastructure, or newly-registered domains showing cryptomining characteristics. Correlate with user click-through logs to establish exposure scope.

suggestion.title: Cryptojacking Malware Execution Post-Redirect
suggestion.rationale: Article describes users redirected to 'Cryptojacking Malware Sites' — this implies binary execution, process injection, or in-browser mining script execution post-compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on execution of known cryptominer binaries (monero, xmrig variants), process injection into legitimate applications, or spawning of resource-intensive background processes with high CPU/GPU utilization and network traffic to mining pools. Monitor for disable of Windows Defender or antivirus services.

suggestion.title: Prompt Injection / Chatbot Service Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Attack required compromise or manipulation of chatbot recommendation logic — whether via prompt injection, account takeover, or service-level compromise. Pipeline should detect anomalous changes to recommendation outputs or admin-level modifications.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor chatbot service audit logs for unauthorized recommendation list modifications, API key exposure or use from anomalous locations, changes to URL whitelists/recommendation datasets, or sudden volume spikes in recommendation generation for new domains.

suggestion.title: Unusual Cryptocurrency Mining Network Traffic Patterns
suggestion.rationale: Cryptojacking implies sustained outbound connections to mining pools and C2 for command/config updates. Victims should exhibit anomalous network egress.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect persistent outbound traffic to known cryptocurrency mining pool addresses, Monero p2p nodes, or stratum protocol connections on high-numbered ports. Flag DNS queries for pool.supportxmr.com, monero-pool.* domains, or sudden bulk DNS resolution of mining infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Integrity Check: Chatbot AI Model/Service Tampering
suggestion.rationale: If compromise occurred at the chatbot service provider level (model poisoning, backend infrastructure), this represents supply-chain attack detection need. Article describes systematic redirection, implying systemic rather than individual-account compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baselines for chatbot response consistency across time and cohorts; detect model updates or retraining with suspicious timing, unauthorized commits to inference logic, or mismatches between deployed model versions and canonical registries.

suggestion.title: Resource Exhaustion / Performance Degradation from Mining
suggestion.rationale: Cryptojacking causes sustained CPU/memory/GPU contention. Endpoints running malware should show anomalous resource utilization and performance complaints.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on sustained high CPU/GPU usage (>80% for >10min) from unsigned/unknown processes; memory pressure; thermal throttling; and correlation with mining malware artifacts or mining pool connections. Cross-reference with user complaints of slowness.

suggestion.title: Exploitation of BadHost Vulnerability Against AI Agent Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states 'Attackers Can Exploit BadHost to Access Sensitive AI Agent Server Endpoints'—this is the core attack vector. No kill-chain phases or detection logic were generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP requests containing BadHost exploit patterns or known CVE payloads targeting AI agent framework endpoints. Alert on successful responses (200/201) to suspicious endpoint paths like /agent/config, /agent/api, /ai/credentials following failed authentication or suspicious User-Agent strings.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Access to AI Agent Server Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Title specifies 'Access to Sensitive AI Agent Server Endpoints'—implies successful post-exploitation access. No use case captures endpoint-level access anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect enumeration or access to known AI agent sensitive endpoints (/api/agents, /api/keys, /api/models, /admin) from source IPs not in whitelist. Flag requests with missing/invalid bearer tokens followed by successful authentication, indicating potential token replay or credential compromise post-BadHost exploitation.

suggestion.title: BadHost-Related Malware or Tool Execution
suggestion.rationale: BadHost is named as the exploit vector. No process execution, file write, or binary signing alerts generated despite this being a likely payload delivery mechanism.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on execution of processes spawned from web-accessible paths, downloads with BadHost-related signatures, or scripts calling AI agent endpoints. Monitor for unsigned executables or scripts writing to temp directories followed by immediate network connections to cloud AI services.

suggestion.title: Password Spray Attack Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'Password spraying attacks rely on exploiting that tendency'—identifies password spray as a material threat to AD environments. Requires detection of authentication anomalies characteristic of spray campaigns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag account lockouts or multiple failed authentication attempts in short time windows. Monitor for patterns: 5+ failed logins on single account within 15 minutes, or 10+ failed attempts across different accounts from single source within 10 minutes. Reduce false positives by excluding locked-out users in credential reset workflows.

suggestion.title: Known Compromised Credential Usage
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes 'stolen credentials are involved in 44.7% of breaches' (Verizon DBIR) and describes breach password protection service checking against 5.4 billion known-breached passwords. Organizations should detect when accounts/passwords in breach databases are used.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on successful authentication using credentials previously identified in public breach databases. Integrate breach intelligence feeds (HIBP, Specops, others) with identity logs. Flag particularly high-risk scenarios: breached credentials from finance/admin accounts, breached credentials with geographic anomalies, or breached credentials followed by lateral movement.

suggestion.title: Suspicious cpanel_jsonapi_func=redisAble Function Calls in cPanel Logs
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Tracked as CVE-2026-48172, this privilege escalation vulnerability is related to the mishandling of Redis enable/disable features and was found in the lsws.redisAble function.' and provides detection command 'grep -rE "cpanel_jsonapi_func=redisAble" /var/cpanel/logs /usr/local/cpanel/logs/'. Pipeline extracted zero use cases from this explicit IOC.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor /var/cpanel/logs and /usr/local/cpanel/logs for references to cpanel_jsonapi_func=redisAble, indicating attempts to invoke the vulnerable Redis enable/disable handler. False positives unlikely; any detection warrants immediate privilege escalation review and IP source attribution.

suggestion.title: LiteSpeed cPanel Plugin Version Detection – Vulnerable Ranges v2.3–v2.4.4
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies: 'This vulnerability is being actively exploited, and poses a risk for all user-end plugin versions between v2.3 and v2.4.4.' Pipeline must identify running versions in /usr/local/cpanel or package manifest to detect vulnerable deployments.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query system package managers, file metadata, and cPanel plugin directories for LiteSpeed cPanel plugin versions in range 2.3–2.4.4. Parse plugin version strings from /usr/local/cpanel/plugins/ or WHM installation manifests. Vulnerable versions present = immediate remediation candidate.

suggestion.title: Privilege Escalation to Root via cPanel Daemon Process
suggestion.rationale: Article describes: 'The vulnerability stems from an incorrect privilege assignment weakness that enables remote attackers with no privileges to execute arbitrary scripts with root privileges.' This is explicit privilege escalation (T1548) via unauthenticated API call.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for child processes spawned by cPanel daemon (cpanel, lsws, or WHM services) with egid/euid 0 (root). Cross-reference parent process with access logs to identify if process creation followed HTTP request to cpanel_jsonapi_func endpoint. Legitimate cPanel admin actions typically originate from authenticated sessions.

suggestion.title: Unauthenticated HTTP Requests to cPanel JSON-RPC Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers have 'no privileges' yet exploit the flaw, implying the Redis function is reachable without authentication. Monitor for unauthenticated requests to cpanel_jsonapi_func endpoints from external IPs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag HTTP requests to /json-api/ or /cpanel_api2 endpoints with cpanel_jsonapi_func parameter originating from non-internal IP ranges and lacking valid session cookies. Correlation with lsws.redisAble function invocation indicates exploitation attempt.

suggestion.title: LiteSpeed Plugin Command Execution Artifacts
suggestion.rationale: Article notes: 'LiteSpeed released urgent security updates on Thursday to address the flaw, warning users to update the cPanel user-end plugin (bundled with the WHM plugin) to the latest version.' Post-exploitation, attackers execute arbitrary scripts with root. Monitor for script execution originating from LiteSpeed context.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect bash, sh, or perl processes spawned with parent process = LiteSpeed daemon or cPanel/WHM service, running as uid 0, with command arguments containing typical payloads (reverse shells, curl/wget downloads, or outbound connections). Baseline legitimate cPanel automation tasks to minimize false positives.

suggestion.title: Exploitation Validation – Check for Malicious IP Activity in cPanel Logs
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'If this command results in any output, we recommend you examine the IPs in the list, determine if they are valid, and if not, block them. To determine any damage done, examine the system logs for any actions taken by the detected IPs.' Pipeline should generate retrospective hunting rule.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Extract source IPs from grep output of cpanel_jsonapi_func=redisAble in logs. Cross-reference those IPs against subsequent actions in system logs (command execution, file access, privilege changes) within short time window (60–300 seconds post-exploitation). Non-whitelisted IPs indicate post-exploitation reconnaissance or lateral movement.

suggestion.title: Malicious TanStack Package Installation Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'malicious versions of the product to be published to the npm registry' — must detect installation of poisoned TanStack package versions during compromise window.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm install, yarn add, pnpm operations for TanStack package installations. Cross-reference against known malicious version hashes from vendor advisory. Flag version numbers or timestamps misaligned with official release schedule. Check package-lock.json for integrity changes.

suggestion.title: NPM PostInstall Script Execution from Compromised Package
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'malicious versions...to publish credential-stealing malware' — npm postinstall hooks are primary delivery mechanism for supply chain malware execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Node.js process spawning unexpected child processes (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, curl, wget) or network connections during/after npm package installation. Alert on postinstall scripts with atypical resource access, environment variable reads, or credential file access.

suggestion.title: Credential Exfiltration from Development Environment Post-Infection
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'publish credential-stealing malware' — detect exfiltration of secrets from .env, .aws/credentials, SSH keys, and CI/CD tokens typical in development systems.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag file reads of credential stores (.env, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, .docker/config.json, package.json containing secrets) from Node.js processes. Monitor for exfiltration via DNS, HTTP/HTTPS to external domains from development machines. Watch environment variable enumeration preceding network egress.

suggestion.title: NPM Registry Account Compromise or Unauthorized Package Publication
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'malicious versions of the product to be published to the npm registry' — detect registry-level tampering or maintainer account abuse.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm.org account login events for TanStack maintainers outside normal patterns. Alert on packages published outside established release cadence, unusual semver versions, or from non-whitelisted CI/CD IP ranges. Correlate with git commit activity to detect rogue pushes.

suggestion.title: Node.js Child Process Spawning from Development Dependencies
suggestion.rationale: Malware delivered via npm will manifest as suspicious process trees: article describes 'malicious versions' executing within development environments.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor node.exe, npm.exe, yarn.exe for child process spawning to command interpreters or network utilities. Flag base64-encoded commands in process arguments. Alert on Node processes reading /proc or system configuration files. Development systems running TanStack require low thresholds for alerting.

suggestion.title: Package Manifest Tampering or Malicious Version Pinning in CI/CD
suggestion.rationale: Article describes supply chain poisoning — attackers maintain persistence by pinning malicious package versions in package-lock.json across builds.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor package.json and package-lock.json for unexpected version changes, especially downgrades or pre-release versions of TanStack. Alert on commits modifying TanStack entries during compromise window. Correlate with build execution and credential access events in the same timeline.

suggestion.title: Nx Console Extension Installation or Version Change
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'malicious version of Nx Console to be published.' Supply-chain compromise at the extension distribution layer requires detection of installation or upgrade during the vulnerable window.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor VS Code extension directories for Nx Console installation or version changes. Alert on any modifications between compromise disclosure and remediation deadline (2026-06-10). Correlate with user context and deployment workflows.

suggestion.title: Obfuscated Code Execution from VS Code Extension Host
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'fetched an obfuscated payload.' Malicious extension downloads and executes encoded/obfuscated code—detection must flag script spawning with obfuscation markers from extension processes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on PowerShell/cmd/node child processes spawned by VS Code extension host (nodeVsCodeHost.exe, extensionHost.js) with obfuscated command lines (base64, hex, Unicode escapes, concatenation). Correlate with simultaneous outbound network activity.

suggestion.title: Credential Harvesting from Disk
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'harvested credentials from multiple sources on disk.' Detection must capture file system access from extension processes to credential stores: .ssh directories, browser profiles, cloud CLI configs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag file system access from VS Code extension host to sensitive credential directories: ~/.ssh, %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Credentials, ~/AppData/Local/Google/Chrome/User Data, .aws/credentials, .azure, .gcloud. Alert on rapid enumeration of multiple credential store locations.

suggestion.title: Credential Harvesting from Memory
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'harvested credentials from...in memory.' Requires memory access primitives (LSASS dumps, process injection) from extension context—anomalous for a UI extension.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for OpenProcess/ReadProcessMemory/QuerySystemInformation API calls from VS Code extension host targeting LSASS, services.exe, or svchost.exe. Alert on PROCESS_VM_READ or PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION access with credential-dumping patterns.

suggestion.title: Network Exfiltration of Harvested Credentials
suggestion.rationale: Stolen credentials must be exfiltrated. Article does not specify C2, but abnormal outbound traffic from development tools carrying credential-like data is high-confidence signal.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on outbound connections from VS Code extension processes to non-standard destinations (non-GitHub/npm/VS Code ASNs or TLDs). Inspect payloads for credential patterns: bearer tokens, PEM headers, email:password pairs, API key prefixes.

suggestion.title: Package Inventory and Hash Verification Against CISA Advisory
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain compromise at distribution requires validation of installed versions. Article specifies malicious versions were published and federal remediation deadline is 2026-06-10.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query endpoint inventory for Nx Console extension versions and file hashes. Cross-reference against CISA advisory for malicious version ranges. Flag any installations in the vulnerable window (before remediation deadline).

suggestion.title: Vulnerable Daemon Tools Lite Detected (CVE-2026-8398)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'Standard asset-exposure hunt' and instructs 'match against your vulnerability scanner.' Pipeline generated zero use cases despite this direct guidance and CISA KEV priority.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query vulnerability scanners (SCCM, Qualys, Tenable) for systems reporting CVE-2026-8398. Correlate with software inventory (WMI Win32_Product, Registry HKLM\Software\Daemon Tools Lite) to identify installations prior to 2026-05-30 (federal patch deadline). Escalate any systems still vulnerable post-deadline as non-compliance risk.

suggestion.title: Child Process Execution from Daemon Tools Installation
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'embedded malicious code' with C/I/A impact. Pipeline ignored execution stage. Once installed, malicious code must execute—detection should look for suspicious child processes spawned from Daemon Tools directories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for processes spawned from typical Daemon Tools paths (C:\Program Files\Daemon Tools*\) or from its registry-launched auto-start entries. Flag LOLBin children (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, cscript.exe, msiexec.exe, regsvcs.exe). Correlate with parent process hash to detect if Daemon Tools binary itself is unsigned or hash-mismatched against known-good versions.

suggestion.title: Network Beaconing from Daemon Tools Process
suggestion.rationale: Article states impact on 'confidentiality, integrity, and availability'—suggesting C2 or data exfiltration. Pipeline missed command-and-control indicators. Daemon Tools is a CD emulation tool; any outbound C2 is malicious.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTP/HTTPS/DNS connections from Daemon Tools process (or children) to non-whitelisted external IPs/domains. Establish baseline: Daemon Tools does not require internet connectivity. High-confidence signal: connections to known C2 infrastructure, high-entropy domain names, or repeated failed connection attempts.

suggestion.title: Trojanized Daemon Tools Installer Distribution
suggestion.rationale: Article indicates vulnerability is 'embedded' in the product—implying supply chain compromise at build/distribution stage. Pipeline detected no installer-stage indicators or supply chain compromise hunting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate installer execution (Daemon Tools*.exe, *.msi) with anomalous follow-on behavior: UAC bypass attempts, modification of system binaries, WMI/COM registration, persistence mechanisms (Run keys, scheduled tasks). Cross-reference installer file hash against known-good releases. Detect unsigned or incorrectly signed executables in Daemon Tools installation directories.

suggestion.title: File System Persistence from Daemon Tools Malicious Code
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'embedded malicious code' with availability impact. Pipeline ignored persistence and file-system indicators that would follow initial execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for new Run/RunOnce registry keys or startup folders written by Daemon Tools or its child processes post-installation. Look for file writes to system directories (%SYSTEM%, %SYSTEMROOT%) or suspicious DLL injection into auto-start extensibility points (AppInit_DLLs, LSA providers). Correlate with process ancestry to confirm Daemon Tools origin.

suggestion.title: Daemon Tools Malicious Code Performing Lateral Movement or C2 Staging
suggestion.rationale: Article's C/I/A impact suggests multi-stage attack. Pipeline generated no detection for discovery, lateral movement, or collection phases that would follow successful execution on initial victim.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for reconnaissance activity (net.exe, ipconfig, tasklist, wmic) executed by or as children of Daemon Tools processes. Detect SMB/RPC scanning from compromised host to other systems, or credential dumping attempts (lsass.exe access, registry hive reads). High-fidelity signal: these tools invoked with non-interactive parent process trees.

suggestion.title: Automated API Surface Probing - High Request Volume to Multiple Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Autonomous attackers are already probing application surfaces continuously at machine speed' and describes pentesting motion as 'recon, probe, observe' — this is systematic reconnaissance behavior detectable via request pattern analysis.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Single source entity making rapid sequential requests to distinct API endpoints or parameters within narrow time window, characteristic of automated discovery. Baseline: typical user requests to 3–5 endpoints/day; anomaly threshold: >50 unique endpoint/parameter combinations in 1 hour.

suggestion.title: Authorization Boundary Testing - Systematic Cross-Object Access Attempts
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes BOLA detection works via 'chain of authorization probes guided by structural reasoning about how API objects relate to identities' and mentions 'User A should not be able to read user B's invoice' as context-dependent vulnerability — systematic testing of object-access permissions is detectable.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Single authenticated session or service-account attempting access to multiple distinct object IDs or tenant namespaces sequentially, particularly when access is denied or returns 403/401 errors followed by retry with modified parameters (e.g., different user_id, account_id, tenant_id).

suggestion.title: Cross-Tenant or Cross-User Data Leakage Attempts - Lateral Object Enumeration
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies 'cross-tenant data leakage, authentication bypasses' as context-dependent vulnerabilities and notes 'BOLA or IDOR' have no heuristic signature but can be found through systematic testing of access boundaries.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Session or API key iterating through sequential or enumerated object identifiers (invoice_id, user_id, org_id) across tenant/ownership boundaries, returning 200 OK responses that suggest successful unauthorized access to resources not owned by the requester's identity.

suggestion.title: Chained Vulnerability Exploitation Sequence - Multi-Stage Attack Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'chained vulnerabilities, where a couple of mediums and highs combine into a critical exploit path' exist in the gap between intended and actual behavior — orchestrated sequences of exploit steps are distinct from single-vulnerability attempts and warrant separate detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Sequence of 2+ requests from same source that together satisfy preconditions for escalation: e.g., (1) auth bypass attempt + (2) privilege-escalation probe + (3) data exfiltration request, where intermediate responses suggest attacker is adapting behavior based on previous response (not blind scanning).

suggestion.title: AI-Driven Continuous Attack Surface Reconnaissance - Sustained Automated Probing Pattern
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes 'the race at hand is now whether your offensive security testing finds the flaws before an attacker's offensive AI does' and 'Autonomous attackers are already probing application surfaces continuously at machine speed, on a schedule defenders can't keep up with' — this describes sustained, pattern-breaking reconnaissance distinct from point-in-time scans.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Source IP or User-Agent showing probing activity (varied payloads, sequential endpoint requests, parameter fuzzing) sustained over hours/days with minimal human-like delay patterns; entropy of request distribution and response-driven branching (attacker changes next request based on prior response) suggest automated reasoning-loop activity rather than static scanning.

suggestion.title: API Parameter Fuzzing and Injection Testing - Automated Vulnerability Search Pattern
suggestion.rationale: Article discusses SQL injection, XSS as 'heuristic-detectable' and implies attackers are testing for both known signatures and context-dependent flaws via automated means; sustained fuzzing of API parameters is a distinct attack behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Single source systematically varying parameter values (type, encoding, length, special characters) against same endpoint, testing for error signatures or behavioral changes indicative of injection vulnerability; combined with high request volume per endpoint and low success-rate ratio of 200 responses.

suggestion.title: Suspicious IT Support Phishing Email Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'SRG actors...send phishing emails to urge employees to call the SRG actor posing as IT support.' Email-based initial contact is the first observable attack step.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify inbound emails with IT support or helpdesk impersonation language requesting callback, credential verification, or urgent action. Monitor subject lines and body content matching common support themes ('verify account', 'confirm identity', 'call IT now'). Flag emails from external domains with IT-related terminology and high urgency markers.

suggestion.title: Remote Desktop Access Grant Following Social Engineering
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'directs the employee to grant access to a remote desktop session.' RDP access grants are observable in endpoint and security logs and represent critical execution phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect RDP or remote desktop access grants to user accounts within hours of phishing emails or suspicious phone contact. Alert on first-time remote access from non-corporate IP ranges, unusual geographies, or outside business hours. Flag accounts with no prior remote access history receiving access requests.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized In-Person Physical Access Claiming IT Support
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies: 'SRG sends a threat actor to the victim's location to gain access' and lists 'presence of unidentified or unauthorized individuals claiming to be IT support' as an indicator. Physical access attempts are detectable via security and access controls.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on unidentified individuals accessing secure floors or server rooms claiming IT support roles. Cross-reference badge logs against known IT staff rosters and on-site employee lists. Flag badge uses without proper authorization workflows, individuals without escort requirements, or access attempts during off-hours.

suggestion.title: USB or External Storage Device Insertion and Rapid Data Transfer
suggestion.rationale: Article describes: 'connect USB drives or external hard drives to the victim's computer' and lists 'unauthorized installation of external hard drives or USB drives' as an SRG indicator. Device insertion and bulk data movement are observable exfiltration signals.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for USB or external drive connections on endpoints, especially following suspicious RDP sessions or physical security incidents. Alert on large data transfers (>500MB) to removable media within 1-hour windows. Flag unauthorized external drives appearing in device inventory alongside anomalous file access patterns.

suggestion.title: Typosquatted IT Support Portal Domain Registration and Web Access
suggestion.rationale: Article reveals: 'register domains to impersonate IT helpdesk or support portals for major U.S. law firms...using typosquatted patterns.' Infrastructure patterns are observable in DNS queries, web proxies, and domain registrations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify DNS requests to domains with typosquatted patterns mimicking legitimate law firm or bank IT support sites. Alert on newly registered domains with minor character variations of known targets and IT-related keywords. Monitor for user credential submissions to these domains.

suggestion.title: Ransom Extortion Communication via Email and Phone
suggestion.rationale: Article notes: 'ransom email that threatens to sell or post it on their leak site, and will also call the victims' employees or clients to pressure them.' Post-compromise extortion communications are observable and indicative of successful data theft.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect emails containing ransom language, threats to publish data, or demands for payment. Monitor for coordinated phone calls to employees and clients with similar extortion messaging. Alert on bulk email distribution with data-leak threats or references to specific company data.

suggestion.title: Lookalike Domain Registration — FIFA World Cup Theme
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly references '300+ Fake Domains' targeting FIFA fans; pipeline extracted zero domain IOCs. Any phishing campaign of this scale should surface domains mimicking legitimate sports/betting/ticketing sites.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor domain registration for lookalike variants of FIFA, World Cup, official ticketing, and major sports betting domains. Flag newly registered or recently seen domains containing 'fifa', 'worldcup', 'ticket', combined with typosquatting patterns (e.g., 'f1fa', 'worlcup') and check against passive DNS for rapid subdomain sprawl.

suggestion.title: Phishing Email — Sporting Event Credential Harvest
suggestion.rationale: Campaign name and targeting profile ('FIFA World Cup fans') indicates spearphishing or mass phishing emails. No email-based detection use cases generated despite obvious social engineering vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect emails with FIFA/World Cup urgency themes (ticket sales, free access, account verification) containing external URLs or form submissions. Correlate with user clicks and subsequent credential submissions via HTTP POST to unfamiliar domains.

suggestion.title: Suspicious URL Click — Phishing Landing Page Access
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline generated no detection rules for endpoint or email gateway logging of user interaction with phishing URLs, despite this being the critical credential-harvesting moment in the kill chain.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when users click embedded URLs in emails that resolve to newly-registered, lookalike, or previously-unseen domains. Correlate with credential submission events (form POST) or account compromise indicators within 1 hour.

suggestion.title: Web Form Credential Submission — Phishing Landing Page
suggestion.rationale: Title and campaign name indicate credential-harvesting phishing, but no detection for the harvesting payload itself (fake login forms, fake ticket purchase forms capturing payment or identity data).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP POST requests to lookalike/newly-registered domains containing credential-like form fields (username, password, email, payment card, FIFA account). Baseline legitimate sporting-event sites to exclude.

suggestion.title: Domain Name Typosquatting Pattern — FIFA Variants
suggestion.rationale: 300+ domains implies systematic domain generation or bulk typosquatting. Pipeline did not reconstruct the naming pattern (e.g., character omission, numeric substitution, TLD variation) to enable broad detection across similar variants.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Ingest domain registration feeds and known lookalike/typosquat domain lists; flag registration clusters where multiple domains registered within short timeframe share FIFA/World Cup keywords and common typo patterns (e.g., 'ficfa', 'fifa-tickets', 'worldcuptickets-2024'). Cross-reference against WHOIS registrant patterns.

suggestion.title: Email Gateway — GHOST STADIUM Campaign Detection
suggestion.rationale: Campaign identified by name ('GHOST STADIUM') in title; no intelligence-driven email rule or threat-name alert generated. If campaign IOCs (sender domains, payloads, URL signatures) exist, email gateways should have campaign-specific detection rules.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Create email filter rule for GHOST STADIUM campaign based on extracted IOCs (sender domains, subject line patterns, URL domains). Alert on message volume spikes from new senders with FIFA-themed subjects pointing to extracted domains.

suggestion.title: Yamcs authentication privilege abuse — ChangeMissionDatabase role assumption by non-admin accounts
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'authenticated user with ChangeMissionDatabase privilege' is the prerequisite for exploitation. No hunt detects abnormal privilege assumption or role abuse.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for successful authentication to Yamcs with subsequent role elevation or ChangeMissionDatabase privilege assignment outside normal administrative patterns. Look for rapid privilege assumption post-authentication or privilege grant by non-admin accounts.

suggestion.title: Janino compilation errors and reflection abuse in Java application logs
suggestion.rationale: Article cites 'Janino Expression Engine' and dynamic compilation. No hunt targets Janino-specific logging such as compilation failures, ClassNotFoundException, reflection access, or bytecode generation errors.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt Yamcs/Java application logs for Janino compilation exceptions, reflection method invocations on Runtime or ProcessBuilder classes, dynamic class loading, or bytecode manipulation attempts. Successful code injection often leaves traces in stack traces or exception logs.

suggestion.title: Yamcs algorithm definition modification outside expected maintenance windows
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'dynamically compiles and evaluates user-controlled algorithm text.' No hunt detects file-based algorithm config tampering outside the UC_33_5 API PATCH detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for creation, modification, or deletion of algorithm definition files (.xml, .algo, or Yamcs config files) outside change-control windows. Correlate file modifications with authentication events to identify suspicious algorithm updates.

suggestion.title: System enumeration and information discovery from Yamcs Java process
suggestion.rationale: Article lists T1082 (System Information Discovery) as an observed technique, but no hunt targets post-RCE enumeration (whoami, uname, ifconfig) spawned by Yamcs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for child processes of Yamcs/Java executing system reconnaissance commands (whoami, hostname, uname, ip addr, systemctl list-units, etc.). Pair with UC_33_4 to detect discovery-phase activity post-shell spawning.

suggestion.title: Algorithm text payload inspection — inline Java/reflection/ProcessBuilder syntax in database
suggestion.rationale: Core vulnerability: 'no secure sandbox' for algorithm evaluation. No hunt inspects algorithm definition content for dangerous Java patterns like Runtime.exec(), ProcessBuilder, or reflection invocations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt Yamcs database or configuration storage for algorithm definitions containing dangerous keywords (Runtime, ProcessBuilder, getRuntime, exec, reflect, Method.invoke, ClassLoader). Correlate with PATCH requests to algorithm endpoints.

suggestion.title: Liquid template filter chain injection in HTTP request bodies
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly demonstrates SSTI via filter piping: `1|valueOf` and references `r.liquid.parser`, `getBuiltinModule`, `child_process`. High-entropy filter chaining in POST/GET parameters is a direct exploitation vector not captured as a standalone hunt.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag HTTP requests containing suspicious Liquid filter syntax (|valueOf, |inspect, |first, |last chains) especially in template or parameter fields. High entropy filter sequences in URL-encoded or JSON payloads are anomalous for legitimate templating.

suggestion.title: JavaScript __proto__ prototype pollution gadget tokens in HTTP requests
suggestion.rationale: The article's SPL/KQL explicitly hunt for `assign%20__proto__` and `__proto__` strings, indicating prototype pollution is part of the gadget chain. This deserves a dedicated UC to detect the pollution vector independently.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTP requests containing `__proto__` assignment, especially in template tags or parameter names. Prototype pollution is a common gadget for breaking sandbox restrictions in JS template engines.

suggestion.title: Node.js spawning unexpected interpreter processes without prior HTTP logging
suggestion.rationale: UC_9_3 detects Node→shell spawning but assumes HTTP context. Gaps exist if the RCE child process is spawned and executes before HTTP logging completes, or if process spawn occurs asynchronously. A process-centric view independent of HTTP is needed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect cmd.exe, powershell, sh, bash, etc. spawned by node.exe or w3wp.exe with parent process lifetime <5 seconds, indicating synchronous RCE execution. Exclude common legitimate patterns (npm install, build scripts).

suggestion.title: Yamcs MdbOverrideApi algorithm PATCH with Java.type RCE payload
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'Nashorn ScriptEngine used to evaluate user-supplied algorithm text in MdbOverrideApi.updateAlgorithm' and lists indicators: 'Java.type', 'java.lang.Runtime', 'getRuntime', 'ProcessBuilder'. PATCH to /api/mdb-overrides/*/algorithms/* is the attack surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Look for PATCH requests to /api/mdb-overrides/*/algorithms/* endpoints where request body contains Nashorn RCE signatures: Java.type(), Runtime.getRuntime(), ProcessBuilder, or /dev/tcp/ references. Correlate with ChangeMissionDatabase privilege or guest user account.

suggestion.title: Java process (Yamcs) spawning shell interpreter
suggestion.rationale: Article states that after Nashorn script evaluation, attacker can 'execute arbitrary Java code', leading to shell spawning. Post-exploitation phase: 'Yamcs JVM spawning a POSIX shell — Nashorn Runtime.exec post-exploitation'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on java process with yamcs/org.yamcs in command line spawning bash, sh, dash, zsh, nc, ncat, socat, python, or perl. Parent-child relationship between Java and shell is the critical signal.

suggestion.title: Reverse shell via /dev/tcp from Yamcs process tree
suggestion.rationale: Article describes post-exploitation: 'Reverse-shell /dev/tcp file descriptor from Yamcs java process tree' as distinct C2 indicator. Quote: ProcessCommandLine checking for '/dev/tcp/' or '/dev/udp/'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect bash/sh/zsh spawned with /dev/tcp/[IP]/[PORT] or /dev/udp/ in the command line where parent is Java or grandparent is Java with yamcs-related process names. Extract remote IP and port for C2 attribution.

suggestion.title: Yamcs default guest user with ChangeMissionDatabase privilege exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'In Yamcs's default configuration (no security.yaml), the built-in guest user [can exploit this].' This is the privilege-escalation / initial-access vector that the pipeline missed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on successful authentication as 'guest' or default accounts to Yamcs, followed by PATCH requests to MdbOverrideApi endpoints. Flag instances where security.yaml is absent or guest privilege is not restricted.

suggestion.title: Nashorn ClassFilter bypass via ScriptEngine instantiation
suggestion.rationale: Root cause from article: 'ScriptEngine used to evaluate user-supplied algorithm text... constructed without a ClassFilter'. This is the vulnerability mechanism — detection should cover missing security controls.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt Yamcs server logs for Nashorn ScriptEngine instantiation or algorithm evaluation errors. Flag any eval() or script execution from untrusted algorithm definitions. Also check for presence of ClassFilter in Yamcs config; absence is a vulnerability signal.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Private Container Image Pull Without Credentials
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states vulnerability 'exposes private container images without authentication'—core attack path is unauthenticated registry access.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor container registry (Docker, OCI, Gitea) for pull/fetch operations to private image repositories where the request lacks valid Bearer token, OAuth session, or authentication headers. Flag successful 200/201 responses to private namespace pulls from unauthenticated clients.

suggestion.title: Gitea API Token/Session Bypass Detection
suggestion.rationale: Vulnerability mechanism likely involves session/token validation bypass in Gitea API endpoints handling container manifest access—'without authentication' suggests auth check is skipped or fooled.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HTTP requests to Gitea `/v2/` (Docker Registry API v2) or container manifest endpoints that lack `Authorization` header or contain malformed/expired tokens, yet receive 200 OK responses. Track requests from IPs without prior valid authentication events.

suggestion.title: Mass Container Image Enumeration Against Private Gitea Registry
suggestion.rationale: Vulnerability disclosure likely enables attackers to enumerate private image tags/versions without auth—'exposes' implies discoverability, not just download access.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for rapid sequential requests to Gitea container registry tag/manifest listing endpoints (e.g., `/v2/<namespace>/<repo>/tags/list`, `/catalog`) from single source IP within short time window, especially if unauthenticated or from non-whitelisted CIDR. Flag if requests probe multiple private namespaces.

suggestion.title: Gitea Container Registry Requests from External/Unexpected Networks
suggestion.rationale: Private container images are typically pulled only by authorized CI/CD systems or internal container orchestrators—unsolicited external registry pulls are anomalous.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline of IPs/ASNs pulling from private Gitea registries; alert on image pull requests originating from non-whitelisted external networks or suspicious geolocations. Correlate with auth bypass attempts.

suggestion.title: Abuse of Gitea Webhook or Deploy Token Disclosure
suggestion.rationale: If vulnerability leaks webhook URLs, deploy tokens, or integration secrets stored in Gitea, attackers gain persistent registry access—common side-effect of auth-bypass bugs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Gitea admin/settings logs for enumeration of webhooks, deploy keys, or token settings by non-admin accounts or during suspected vulnerability exploitation windows. Alert on disclosure of secrets in HTTP request logs or error messages.

suggestion.title: Gitea Version-Specific Vulnerability Exploitation Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Once CVE version range is disclosed, exploitation attempts will target specific Gitea versions via manifest endpoint anomalies—should detect pre/post-patch behavior deltas.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: After CVE disclosure, monitor Gitea server logs for requests matching known exploitation signatures (e.g., path traversal in manifest fetch, parameter injection in auth checks). Correlate with Gitea version in Server headers; alert if vulnerable versions respond to bypass attempts.

suggestion.title: Malicious VS Code/OpenVSX Extension Installation and Activation
suggestion.rationale: Article states extensions 'stole cryptocurrency wallets and developer credentials' and 'planted dozens of dormant extensions on OpenVSX that would activate the malicious component after an update.' Dormancy + update-triggered execution is a critical attack pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on VS Code extension directory writes followed by process spawn only after restart or package update event. Flag unsigned extensions or those with network egress in child processes immediately post-install.
